title: Callistus (14 October)
hook: a slave who lost his master's money, worked the mines, and became bishop of Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, Denis, and the hill of Montmartre. Your line was the mountain of martyrs. What did you learn about a place you pass? Day one thousand thirty-five.

A slave in Rome is trusted with his master's money. He runs a kind of bank, and other Christians deposit their savings with him. Then the money is gone. He panics and runs. He's caught, punished, and later sent to labor in the mines of Sardinia. If you were writing a list of future popes, his name would not be on it. And yet some years later, the man from the mines is bishop of Rome. Today, Callistus.
screen: `A SLAVE WITH A BANK.` → `THE MONEY IS GONE.` → `FROM THE MINES TO ROME.`

segments.voice: Much of what we know about Callistus comes from someone who disliked him: Hippolytus, a Roman priest and writer who opposed him bitterly. So read the story with that in mind. The bank failure, the flight, the mines: Hippolytus tells it to make Callistus look bad. Some readers today come away liking Callistus more. Released from Sardinia, he lived quietly outside Rome for a time; later the bishop of Rome, Zephyrinus, took him in, made a deacon, and put in charge of the Christian burial ground on the Appian Way. Those underground galleries still bear his name: the Catacombs of Saint Callistus. Then he was chosen bishop of Rome himself. Here's what made Hippolytus so angry. Callistus allowed Christians who had committed serious sins, and had done penance, to be welcomed back to communion. Hippolytus thought that was far too soft. Cornelius would face the same question after him. Some readers see Callistus's own story in his answer: a man who had failed with other people's money, been punished, and been given a second chance, now keeping the door open for others. In Matthew, Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive. Seven times? The answer, in the Douay-Rheims: "I say not to thee, till seven times; but till seventy times seven times." Tradition says Callistus died a martyr. And the end of the feud is worth knowing: tradition says Hippolytus, in time, was reconciled to the Church and also died a martyr. The Church now honors them both as saints. The angry critic and the forgiving shepherd ended up on the same calendar.
screen: `HIS STORY COMES FROM A RIVAL.` · `KEEPER OF THE CATACOMBS.` · `HE WELCOMED BACK THOSE WHO REPENTED.` · `BOTH MEN BECAME SAINTS.` · then, large: `SEVENTY TIMES SEVEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone who's failed. Get comfortable and breathe. Think of a person who let you down, or let others down, and has tried to make it right. Notice whether there's a door in you still shut against them. You don't have to fling it open. Just see if it could open a crack. If you pray, you can bring them before God by name. If you don't, simply picture greeting them warmly, once. The bell holds the time.
Callistus. A slave who failed, was punished, came back, kept the catacombs, and as bishop of Rome welcomed back sinners who repented.
Your line: from slave to shepherd. Today, when someone's old mistake comes up, mention who they are now instead. Day one thousand thirty-five.

howItsDone: Pope Saint Callistus I is remembered on 14 October; in Rome, pilgrims visit the Catacombs of Saint Callistus on the Appian Way.

fork.setup: you're Zephyrinus, bishop of Rome. a former slave turns up, back from the Sardinian mines, with a failed bank behind him. what do you do?
options: send him away: he can't be trusted
make him a deacon and put him in charge of the burial ground
let him come to church, but give him no work
fork.reveal: Zephyrinus took him in, made him a deacon and gave him the cemetery on the Appian Way, which still bears his name.

Audit: in Hippolytus (Refutation 9.12) Victor first sent the freed Callistus to Antium on an allowance and only later did Zephyrinus bring him back, so 'after his release ... taken in by Zephyrinus' is now 'lived quietly outside Rome for a time; later Zephyrinus took him in'.
